title: Defining Creoles and color in New Orleans
summary: Tex gives his definition of Creole, discusses Marie Laveau, the Autocrat Club, color prejudice and the Seventh Ward.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: You brought up, well, this may be a little much, we're just sort of crisscrossing here. Creoles, Creole blacks. What was your feeling about the relationship of the Creoles?
Well, I think that... Creoles in New Orleans... That's going to be, that's going to have to be another tape.
Well, can we start? Can we start?

Yeah, well, you see, when you start thinking about the Creoles, you see, from the black side, you've got one ideology about Creoles. Then on the, black side, you've got one, white side, you've got another. The way I see it, it was an intermixture, a combination of white, Spaniards and blacks that made up the Creole from the black side. But on the white side, you've got whites who, shall we say, limited their sexual or interrelationship with French-born black women to develop a Creole. You see, you're dealing with a metaphysical as well as a physical kind of thing, which also will give you a, shall we say, a socialized definition according to who is writing or who is talking about it. Well,
what, do we have, can we have a definition of Creole?
Well, I can give you my definition of it.
Oh, give me your definition?
My definition is a combination of black, Spanish, French, and Indian that makes up a Creole. The ones that I know.
You need all those four elements.

You need those four elements to make up a Creole. You're talking about French, Spanish, black, in conjunction with, of course, with whites and Indian, maybe four or five. This is the way I see it now. You take like Marie Laveau. Marie Laveau was a Creole. See, Marie Laveau was part French and black. Her daddy was a Frenchman. Her mother was part black and part Indian, the way it was told to me. So, she was a Creole. My, my, my original God for the first time I was baptized was a Creole. He was black. Ijean de Plessis, which is French and black. That's when I was christened the first time. Second time I had a, a, a black person. You know, that's when I came into adulthood when I was baptized, you see. So, I don't know. It, it all depends on who's talking and who's writing as to what is a, who's a Creole. How do you dignify it? Of course now, they, they, they so-called sophisticated, I wouldn't say the sophisticated, well, the poor whites who know about the term or usage of Creole do not want to be identified with blacks as Creoles. You see, because,
don't want blacks to have that identity.

Right, they don't want to have that identity because, you see, they are still whites, like the other day I was talking about what was happening on cyberspace with all this stuff put on by the white citizen council and the clans they got.
On the internet?
On the internet.
Right.

And, you know, like the situation that's happening out in Missouri right now where they've taken on acres of land and they've set this thing up as a totally white thing there. No blacks, no Jews, you know, no Catholics in there. So, this is the situation. Who's talking about a Creole? What is a Creole? Now, most Creoles, a lot of people think Creoles got to be high yellow with straight cold black hair but all Creoles are not like. There are black Creoles who have, who are jet black with beautiful Italian or Indian type hair with beautiful features and they stand up and look like midnight. And then, you got other Creoles who have the Caucasian, Caucasianized kind of look which is accepted by the so-called white because this type of Creole can pass and identify with him from the Caucasian or angle. But now, the real dark and the true Creole who has the dark complexion, that's another thing. It's just like a case we have in the courts of Louisiana about this woman had a birth certificate where she was black but the woman really is a Caucasian type individual with somebody in the court made a mistake and she can't get that knocked off of her record and it's having a problem with her family on this kind of thing. So, it all depends on who's writing and who's talking.
the relationship, the social relationship as far as discrimination of the Creoles, the Seventh Ward, the Creoles as we talk about.

Well, at one time, well today you have what is known as the Autocrat Club. It's still there on San Bernard Avenue and in the very beginning they were sort of highlighted to, shall we say, administer socially to the Creoles or high yalas of color to become members or if you were my complexion with the kind of hair I've had. You wasn't too accepted in thought but today it's a different kind of thing because you had that Seventh Ward and Eighth Ward kind of Creole who had the, shall we say, the Caucasian type hair and the Caucasian type features was accepted and let's face it, white folks really accept the, accept the people my complexion I guess in deference to somebody who sort of looked like the bass of this microphone which is very black. So, you still have a color thing today. All right, you take, let's look at television today. Very few people of dark complexion do you have on television. All of the blacks that you see on television in most cases have the Caucasian or type, a light complexion or Creole kind of features on television. Color has a lot of bearing on how far you elevate in life sometimes. Even today as we go into the 21st century, this is revolting as hell and yet I know some people who black as midnight make a heck of a lot of money and I know some people who are limited in education can very, can't really talk too well but to handle a heck of a lot of money. I can think of a young man who passed some time ago trying to think of his name right now who made a heck of a lot of money in junk.
Yeah.
He's dead today but he couldn't handle the king's English as such but he made a lot of money and he financed and paid a lot of taxes right here in the city.
